title: Why do we yawn?
subtitle: Body & brain
subject: sciences
description: Everyone yawns: humans, dogs, sometimes even unborn babies. It is probably not about running short of oxygen. Here are the strongest leads.

hero.hook: You yawn. Your neighbor yawns. And that is (almost) no accident.

blocks.text: A yawn looks trivial. In fact it is a complex reflex: jaw, chest, diaphragm, the whole body joins in. Lions, dogs, humans: plenty of animals yawn.
For a long time people said, “It's to get more oxygen.” That idea has now been largely dropped. The modern explanations are far more interesting.
Experiments have shown that adding oxygen to the air does not stop people from yawning. Nor does lowering the carbon dioxide a little. So a yawn is not a simple way of catching up on air.
One strong lead today: yawning may help **regulate brain temperature**. By breathing in deeply and stretching the face, we may ventilate and cool the head a little, especially when we are tired.

blocks.caption: Seeing someone yawn is often enough to trigger the reflex

blocks.text: In humans, seeing, hearing, or even reading the word “yawn” can set one off. This is not dumb copying: it also involves **empathy** and brain circuits tied to [[mirror neurons and contagiousness]], cells that fire when we act, and also when we watch someone else act.
Young children rarely catch a yawn. That sensitivity turns up later, alongside certain social skills.

sections.title: We yawn before we are born

blocks.text: Babies yawn in the womb from about the **11th week** of pregnancy. At that age, their lungs are not breathing air yet. So once again, it is not about running short of oxygen.
Before birth, yawning may help develop the muscles of the jaw and the face.
We often yawn when we are tired, but also just before a test, or when we are bored and trying to stay focused. The stretch may stimulate the nervous system and help us **stay alert**.
A yawn is probably not a sign of missing oxygen. It seems to help regulate the brain, both its temperature and its alertness, and in humans it also spreads by social contagion.
